Likeness is about looking like something or someone. Whether it describes a similarity between two real things, or a picture that represents a person, the word always orbits around one central idea: the quality of resembling something, or something that resembles something else.

Meaning 1 — Resemblance or Similarity

This is the most common meaning. When two people or things share similar features in appearance, you can say there is a likeness between them.

Think of it this way: if two brothers have the same nose, the same eyes, and the same jaw, people might say there is a strong likeness between them. This likeness is the quality they share — the way they look alike.

Examples:

  • "Everyone noticed the likeness between the mother and her daughter."
  • "There is a striking likeness between the two paintings — same style, same colors."
  • "She bears a likeness to her grandmother."

Notice the phrase "bears a likeness to" — this simply means looks similar to. It is one of the most natural ways to use the word.

Key nuance: Likeness here refers specifically to outward, visible similarity — how things look, not how they think or behave. If you say someone's personality is similar to another person's, you would not normally use likeness for that. You would use similarity instead. But if their faces, build, or appearance are alike, likeness fits perfectly.

Meaning 2 — A Portrait, Image, or Representation of a Person

In this meaning, a likeness is a physical object — a painting, photograph, drawing, statue, coin engraving, or any other image — that represents what a person looks like.

Think of it as: a captured image of someone's appearance.

The key idea is that this representation is recognizable — it actually looks like the person it depicts. A bad painting that doesn't look like the person at all would not be called a good likeness.

Examples:

  • "The artist painted a remarkable likeness of the queen."

(= a portrait that truly captured how she looked)

  • "His likeness was printed on the coin."

(= his face/image was stamped onto it)

  • "The statue in the park is said to be an excellent likeness of the general."

(= the statue truly resembles how the general appeared)

  • "The police released a likeness of the suspect."

(= a drawn image — often called a composite likeness — depicting the suspect's face)

You will often see this meaning in slightly formal or literary contexts, especially with phrases like "painted his likeness," "carved her likeness," "captured a likeness," or "sculpted in his likeness."

Meaning 3 — The Form or Outward Appearance of Something (Guise)

This is a more literary and somewhat older use, but it still appears regularly — especially in religious texts, classic literature, and formal writing. Here, likeness means the outward form or shape of something, especially when something takes on the appearance of something else.

Examples:

  • "The angel appeared in the likeness of a man."

(= the angel took on the outward form/appearance of a man)

  • "God created human beings in His own likeness."

(= in His own image and form)

  • "The creature came disguised in the likeness of a wolf."

(= it appeared in the shape/form of a wolf)

In this meaning, likeness describes what something appears to be — its visual form or shape — rather than an actual resemblance between two separate things.

Learning words in phrases (collocations) is one of the best ways to master them. Here are the most important ones for likeness:

"A strong / striking likeness"
→ A very noticeable resemblance.
"There is a striking likeness between the two cousins."

"Bear a likeness to / bear a striking likeness to"
→ To look similar to someone or something.
"This actor bears an uncanny likeness to the president."

"In the likeness of"
→ In the form or image of; shaped to resemble.
"The figurine was carved in the likeness of a warrior."
"He created the character in the likeness of his own father."

"A good / perfect likeness"
→ A portrait or image that truly captures someone's appearance.
"The photograph is a perfect likeness — it looks exactly like her."

"Family likeness"
→ A shared resemblance among members of the same family.
"You can see the family likeness — they all have the same eyes."

"Capture someone's likeness"
→ To successfully represent how someone looks in a painting, photo, or drawing.
"The portrait beautifully captures her likeness."
How Likeness Compares to Similar Words

Since you want a complete understanding, it helps to see how likeness sits alongside words that seem similar:

Likeness vs. Similarity
Similarity is the broader word. It can refer to anything being alike — appearance, behavior, ideas, structure. Likeness is more focused: it almost always refers to visual, outward resemblance. You can say two people have a similarity in the way they think, but you would not say they have a likeness in that sense.

Likeness vs. Resemblance
These two are the closest in meaning and are often interchangeable. However, resemblance is slightly more common in everyday speech, while likeness can feel a touch more formal or literary. Both refer to outward similarity. "There is a resemblance between them" and "There is a likeness between them" mean essentially the same thing.

Likeness vs. Portrait / Image
When likeness means a painted or drawn image of someone, it overlaps with portrait and image. The difference is subtle: likeness stresses that the image actually looks like the person — the word itself carries the implication of accuracy. A portrait is simply a painting of someone, whether it looks like them or not. A likeness is a portrait that captures them.
The Thread That Ties It All Together

No matter which meaning of likeness you encounter, you can always come back to this single thread:

Likeness = looking like something, or something that looks like something.

Whether it is the resemblance between two siblings, a portrait on a wall, or an angel taking human form — the word is always about visible appearance and how closely one thing reflects another.
